triage.name: Bowel Incontinence
triage.reason: Fecal incontinence/encopresis presents with a clear history and exam, with a differential of organic and behavioral causes worth working up.

review_issues: auto-repaired: labs: dropped 'cbc' (not in the reference table)

demographics: More common in women, largely related to obstetric and pelvic floor injury
Prevalence rises with age but it is not a normal part of aging
Occurs in children as encopresis, usually in the setting of chronic constipation
More common in residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities

risk_factors.text: Older age with frailty or limited mobility
Vaginal childbirth, especially with perineal tear or forceps delivery
Chronic constipation with fecal impaction or overflow
Pelvic floor disorders such as pelvic organ prolapse or prior pelvic surgery
Diabetes mellitus with peripheral or autonomic neuropathy
Neurologic disease affecting the sacral nerves or spinal cord

social_history: Residence in a nursing home or long-term care facility
Limited mobility or need for assistance with toileting

chief_complaints.text: I can't hold my stool until I get to the bathroom
I leak stool into my underwear without knowing it
I have accidents in my pants
I have to rush to the toilet and sometimes I don't make it

hpi.onset: Gradual over months, often after childbirth, pelvic surgery, or years of constipation; sometimes sudden after a stroke or spinal injury
hpi.duration: Usually chronic, present for months to years before the patient seeks care
hpi.progression: Often slowly worsens over time; may fluctuate with stool consistency, and episodes are more frequent when stools are loose
hpi.location: Anorectal; leakage noticed in the underwear or on clothing
hpi.quality: Involuntary passage of solid or liquid stool, or staining of underwear with stool
hpi.severity: Ranges from occasional staining to daily loss of solid stool that limits work, social life, and outings
hpi.timing: Episodes occur with urgency, after meals, with coughing or lifting, or at night in more severe disease
aggravating: Urgency that leaves no time to reach a toilet
Not being able to reach a toilet in time
relieving: Firming the stool with diet or medication
Emptying the bowels on a schedule

associated_symptoms.text: Urgency to have a bowel movement
Staining of underwear between bowel movements
Constipation or a feeling of incomplete emptying
Itching or soreness around the anus
Avoiding social activities or leaving home

pertinent_negatives: Travel or sick contacts with diarrhea
Rectal prolapse or a mass protruding from the anus
New back pain or leg weakness

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in the legs or feet

negatives: Loss of sensation in the saddle area

positives.text: Feeling of a bulge or heaviness in the vagina
Low mood or anxiety about accidents

atypical.how_it_differs: Presents as encopresis, usually with chronic constipation and overflow soiling; the child may hide soiled underwear and deny the problem, and the parent often brings the complaint.

May be attributed to aging or dementia and underreported; often coexists with urinary incontinence, immobility, and cognitive impairment, and may present as soiling found by caregivers rather than a complaint.
May first appear in the third trimester or postpartum after a perineal tear or forceps delivery; often improves in the months after delivery but can persist.
May be painless and associated with other neuropathic symptoms such as numbness or tingling in the feet, and with diarrhea from autonomic neuropathy.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may be reluctant to discuss symptoms
general.moderate: Well-appearing but anxious or embarrassed; may wear a pad or protective undergarment
general.severe: Withdrawn or embarrassed, may smell of stool, avoids sitting for long; possibly frail or with limited mobility
general.critical: Not applicable; bowel incontinence itself is not a critical illness, but a toxic or unstable appearance should prompt evaluation for another cause

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perianal skin and underwear or pad
findings.finding: Staining of the perianal skin or undergarment with stool
Erythema, maceration, or excoriation of the perianal skin

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam and assess resting anal sphincter tone
findings.finding: Decreased resting anal tone, suggesting internal anal sphincter weakness

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to squeeze the anal sphincter around the examining finger
findings.finding: Weak voluntary squeeze, suggesting external anal sphincter or pelvic floor weakness
Hard impacted stool in the rectal vault

findings.maneuver: Inspect the examining glove and any stool on it after the rectal exam
findings.finding: Gross blood or melena on the glove

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to strain or bear down while inspecting the anus
findings.finding: Rectal mucosa or full-thickness rectum protruding through the anus
Soft, non-tender abdomen without mass or guarding

findings.maneuver: Test perineal sensation, the anal wink reflex, and lower extremity strength and reflexes
findings.finding: Intact perineal sensation, present anal wink, and normal strength and reflexes

findings.maneuver: Stroke the perianal skin and observe for contraction of the external anal sphincter
Test sensation in the saddle distribution around the anus and perineum
Perform a pelvic exam with the patient straining
findings.finding: Descent of the vaginal walls, cervix, or uterus

findings.maneuver: Perform a pelvic exam when a gynecologic or pelvic floor cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness, adnexal mass, or prolapse

labs.caveat: Thyrotoxicosis can cause chronic diarrhea and urgency that worsen leakage.
Diabetes is a common cause of autonomic and peripheral neuropathy affecting the anorectum.
Only useful when inflammatory bowel disease or colitis is being considered; usually normal in functional incontinence.
Nonspecific; supports an inflammatory or infectious process when that is suspected.
Negative. Required before pelvic imaging or surgery in anyone who could be pregnant.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected sphincter injury, such as after obstetric tear or anorectal surgery

findings.text: Disruption or thinning of the internal anal sphincter
Disruption of the external anal sphincter

imaging.preferred_when: Complex or postsurgical anatomy, or when ultrasound is inconclusive
Symptoms suggest internal intussusception, rectocele, or incomplete evacuation
Red flags such as rectal bleeding, weight loss, anemia, or age-appropriate cancer screening

findings.text: Mucosal inflammation suggesting inflammatory bowel disease
Usually nonspecific; may show a large stool burden in the colon

initial.why: Screens for anemia from occult bleeding and for infection
Assesses hydration and electrolytes, especially if diarrhea or laxative use is prominent
Thyroid disease can cause diarrhea and urgency that worsen leakage
Diabetes is a common cause of the neuropathy that underlies incontinence
Rules out pregnancy before pelvic imaging or surgery

confirmatory.why: Defines sphincter anatomy and identifies a surgically repairable defect
Measures resting and squeeze pressures, rectal sensation, and the rectoanal inhibitory reflex

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory cause when colitis or inflammatory bowel disease is suspected
supporting.only_if: diarrhea with blood, fever, or weight loss

supporting.why: Adds to inflammatory markers when an inflammatory cause is suspected
supporting.only_if: diarrhea with blood, fever, or weight loss

supporting.why: Evaluates the colon for bleeding, inflammation, or neoplasia
supporting.only_if: rectal bleeding, weight loss, anemia, or age-appropriate cancer screening
endoanal ultrasound is inconclusive or prior anorectal surgery distorts anatomy

supporting.why: Looks for structural causes of incomplete evacuation
supporting.only_if: symptoms suggest intussusception, rectocele, or incomplete emptying

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of bowel incontinence
Not needed unless there is epigastric pain suggesting pancreatitis
Not part of the incontinence workup unless urinary symptoms suggest infection
Not routinely needed; reserved for suspected mass, abscess, or acute intra-abdominal process

decision_points: Pregnancy test before pelvic imaging or surgery in anyone who could be pregnant
Digital rectal exam is part of the initial evaluation and guides whether manometry or imaging is needed
Red flags such as rectal bleeding, weight loss, or anemia prompt colonoscopy before attributing symptoms to a functional cause
Sphincter defect on endoanal ultrasound identifies patients who may benefit from surgical repair

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: A rectal or distal colonic tumor can cause urgency, tenesmus, and leakage of mucus or stool, and is the most important organic cause to exclude.
differential.trigger: Rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia, or a new change in bowel habit in an adult

history: Blood mixed with stool or dark stools
exam: Palpable rectal mass on digital rectal exam
Gross blood or melena on the examining glove
imaging: Colonoscopy showing a mass or polyp

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic inflammation of the rectum causes urgency, tenesmus, and leakage of stool or mucus, and can be mistaken for a functional problem.
differential.trigger: Chronic diarrhea with blood, mucus, urgency, or weight loss in a younger patient

history: Extraintestinal symptoms such as joint pain or mouth ulcers
exam: Perianal fistulas, fissures, or skin tags

differential.name: Infectious colitis
differential.why_considered: Acute diarrhea with urgency and leakage can be caused by an infection, especially after antibiotics or travel.

history: Acute onset of watery or bloody diarrhea
Recent antibiotic use, travel, or sick contacts
labs: Positive stool culture or stool PCR for pathogens
imaging: Colonoscopy or CT showing segmental colitis if severe

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Alternating constipation and diarrhea with urgency can lead to leakage, and it is a common functional disorder.

history: Chronic abdominal pain relieved by defecation
No red flags such as bleeding or weight loss
labs: Normal CBC, CRP, and celiac serology

differential.name: Rectal prolapse
differential.why_considered: Full-thickness or mucosal prolapse can cause leakage of mucus and stool, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation.

history: Feeling of a bulge or mass protruding from the anus
exam: Visible protrusion of rectal mucosa on straining

differential.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differential.why_considered: Compression of the cauda equina can cause loss of bowel control along with saddle anesthesia and leg weakness.
differential.trigger: New back pain with saddle numbness, leg weakness, or urinary retention

exam: Weak lower extremity strength or reflexes
labs: Not specific; urgent imaging is key
imaging: MRI of the lumbar spine showing compression of the cauda equina

severity.mild: Occasional staining of underwear or leakage of small amounts of liquid stool, no need for pads, minimal impact on daily activities.
severity.moderate: Regular leakage requiring pads or protective undergarments, urgency that limits outings, some avoidance of social activities.
severity.severe: Daily loss of solid stool, need for adult diapers, significant restriction of work and social life, may require assistance with toileting.
severity.critical: Not applicable; bowel incontinence itself is not a life-threatening condition, but a toxic or unstable appearance should prompt evaluation for another cause.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests an organic cause such as colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or severe colitis; needs prompt evaluation.
Raises concern for malignancy or chronic inflammatory disease.
May indicate occult gastrointestinal bleeding from a tumor or inflammation.

red_flags.finding: New back pain with saddle numbness or leg weakness
red_flags.meaning: Possible cauda equina syndrome; requires urgent imaging.
Suggests infectious or inflammatory colitis; needs stool studies and possibly colonoscopy.
Concerning for anorectal or colorectal malignancy; requires biopsy.

complications.name: Perianal dermatitis
clues: Erythema, maceration, or excoriation around the anus

complications.name: Social isolation and depression
clues: Low mood or anxiety about accidents

complications.name: Pressure ulcers
clues: Moisture and stool on the skin

special_populations.differences: Presents as encopresis, usually with chronic constipation and overflow soiling; the child may hide soiled underwear and deny the problem, and the parent often brings the complaint. Treatment focuses on bowel retraining and disimpaction.

May be attributed to aging or dementia and underreported; often coexists with urinary incontinence, immobility, and cognitive impairment, and may present as soiling found by caregivers rather than a complaint.
May first appear in the third trimester or postpartum after a perineal tear or forceps delivery; often improves in the months after delivery but can persist.
May be painless and associated with other neuropathic symptoms such as numbness or tingling in the feet, and with diarrhea from autonomic neuropathy.

key_questions.question: Can you describe what happens when you leak — is it solid stool, liquid stool, or just staining of your underwear?
key_questions.looking_for: Type and amount of leakage; liquid stool or staining suggests internal sphincter weakness or overflow, solid stool suggests more severe external sphincter or pelvic floor weakness

key_questions.question: Do you feel an urge to go before you leak, or does it happen without any warning?
key_questions.looking_for: Urge incontinence suggests external sphincter or pelvic floor weakness; passive leakage without warning suggests internal sphincter weakness or neuropathy

key_questions.question: How often does this happen, and how long has it been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequency and chronicity; daily leakage of solid stool indicates severe disease, while occasional staining suggests mild disease

key_questions.question: What makes it worse — loose stools, coughing, lifting, or not reaching a toilet in time?
key_questions.looking_for: Aggravating factors that point to stool consistency, pelvic floor weakness, or urgency as the mechanism

key_questions.question: How often do you have a bowel movement, and what is the consistency? Do you strain or feel like you cannot empty completely?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic constipation with impaction or overflow soiling, or diarrhea that overwhelms sphincter control

key_questions.question: Have you had vaginal deliveries? Were there tears, an episiotomy, or forceps or vacuum assistance?
key_questions.looking_for: Obstetric anal sphincter injury, the most common cause in women

key_questions.question: Have you had any surgery on your anus, rectum, or pelvic area?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior anorectal or pelvic surgery that may have damaged the sphincter or pelvic floor

key_questions.question: Do you have any conditions affecting your nerves or spinal cord, such as diabetes, stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, or a spinal injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic disease affecting the sacral nerves or spinal cord

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including laxatives, stool softeners, and anything for diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Laxatives, stool softeners, or antidiarrheals that alter stool consistency and contribute to leakage

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any blood in your stool, unintentional weight loss, or a change in your bowel habits?
key_questions.looking_for: Red flags for colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease that require prompt evaluation

key_questions.question: Do you have new back pain, numbness in the saddle area, or weakness in your legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Cauda equina syndrome or spinal cord compression requiring urgent imaging

key_questions.question: Do you also leak urine, or feel a bulge or heaviness in the vagina?
key_questions.looking_for: Coexisting urinary incontinence or pelvic organ prolapse suggesting a shared pelvic floor disorder

key_questions.question: How much does this affect your daily life, work, and social activities?
key_questions.looking_for: Impact on quality of life and avoidance behaviors that guide treatment intensity

reasoning_points: Involuntary passage of solid or liquid stool, or staining of underwear, that the patient cannot control
Urgency or lack of warning before leakage, distinguishing urge from passive incontinence
Chronic constipation with impaction or overflow soiling as a common mechanism
Obstetric history of perineal tear or forceps delivery, or prior anorectal or pelvic surgery
Neurologic disease such as diabetes, stroke, Parkinson disease, or spinal cord injury affecting the sacral nerves
Digital rectal exam showing reduced resting or squeeze anal tone, or impacted stool
Red flags such as rectal bleeding, weight loss, anemia, or a rectal mass excluded before attributing symptoms to a functional cause
Pregnancy test before pelvic imaging or surgery in anyone who could be pregnant
Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound define sphincter function and anatomy when conservative treatment fails or surgery is considered

easy: Older multiparous woman with leakage after a forceps delivery and a perineal tear
Clear history of urgency and leakage of liquid stool
Digital rectal exam shows reduced anal sphincter tone
Symptoms worsen with loose stools and improve with firming the stool
medium: Older adult with chronic constipation and overflow soiling mistaken for diarrhea
Patient with diabetes and painless leakage plus peripheral neuropathy
Coexisting urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse suggesting a shared pelvic floor disorder
Symptoms attributed to aging or dementia and underreported by the patient
hard: Child with encopresis who hides soiled underwear and denies the problem
Patient with a rectal mass or iron-deficiency anemia where incontinence is a red herring for colorectal cancer
New back pain with saddle numbness and leg weakness suggesting cauda equina syndrome
Postpartum patient with symptoms that overlap with normal postpartum changes
Patient on multiple laxatives whose leakage resolves after medication review
